pos: v. past, 2nd pers. sing. archaic (thou didst crown; thou didst invest with honor and dominion)
etymology: From Old French coroner, to crown, from Latin corona, a wreath or garland of honor; the archaic -est ending marks second-person singular past tense.
biblical_def:
Thou madest him a little lower than the angels; thou crownedst him with glory and honour, and didst set him over the works of thy hands.

Hebrews quotes Psalm 8 to establish one of its central arguments: man was made a little lower than the angels and crowned with glory and honour, given dominion over creation, yet this high calling is not yet seen to be fully realized in fallen experience. Hebrews immediately applies the psalm to Jesus: but we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour (Heb 2:9). The crowning that Psalm 8 ascribes to humanity in its created design is perfectly and finally fulfilled in Christ, the true Man, whose suffering unto death becomes, paradoxically, the very means of his crowning. The archaic thou crownedst draws the reader into intimate address of God himself, the One who both made man for glory and, in the incarnate Son, actually achieved that glory through death and resurrection on behalf of the many sons he brings to glory (Heb 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CROWN: archaic second-person past; thou didst crown, invest with a crown of honor and authority.
webster_full: CROWN, v.t. To invest with a crown; to adorn with honor, dignity, or dominion.
CROWNEDST, archaic 2nd pers. sing. past: thou didst crown; thou didst invest with glory.
Hebrews 2 quotes Psalm 8's crowning of man with glory and honour.
Applied directly to Jesus, crowned through the suffering of death.
Fulfills man's created design in the incarnate, suffering, risen Son.
scriptures: Heb 2:7
Thou madest him a little lower than the angels; thou crownedst him with glory and honour, and didst set him over the works of thy hands:
corruption_summary: A purely anthropocentric reading of Psalm 8's crowning language, applied to human dignity alone without reference to its fulfillment in Christ, misses Hebrews' own inspired interpretation of the psalm.
corruption_paragraphs: It is possible to cite Psalm 8's crowning of man with glory and honour purely as an affirmation of human dignity and potential, detached from Hebrews' own Christological reading of the text.

Hebrews 2:9 supplies the corrective directly: but we see Jesus... crowned with glory and honour. The dignity Psalm 8 ascribes to man is realized not in fallen humanity's own achievement but in the incarnate Son's suffering, death, and exaltation, on behalf of the many sons he brings with him to glory.
roots_summary: Latin corona, a wreath or garland, underlies crown; crownedst simply carries the archaic Authorized Version second-person ending, matching forms like lovedst and madest.
roots_lines: Corona, a wreath of honor, is the Latin root of crown.

Applied directly to Jesus in Hebrews 2:9, crowned through suffering.

pos: n. (a burden; a hindrance or encumbering weight that impedes action)
etymology: From Old French combrer, to hinder, obstruct, related to encumber; ultimately of uncertain Gaulish or Celtic origin.
biblical_def:
How can I myself alone bear your cumbrance, and your burden, and your strife?

Moses speaks this near the end of his life, recounting to the second generation of Israel how, at Horeb, the weight of governing an increasingly numerous and quarrelsome people had grown too great for one man to bear alone. Cumbrance names this burden precisely: not merely the practical labor of judging disputes but the full encumbering weight of a people's strife, their quarrels, complaints, and contentions, piled onto a single leader. This complaint leads directly to the appointment of capable men as heads over the people, wise and understanding and known, each given authority over smaller divisions (Deu 1:13-15), establishing the principle of delegated, plural leadership under God that recurs throughout Scripture, from Jethro's counsel to Moses (Exo 18:17-23) to the appointment of deacons in Acts 6 and elders throughout the New Testament. Cumbrance thus marks the precise moment Scripture identifies as the origin of shared, distributed church and civil leadership, a wise response to an unsustainable concentration of burden in one man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CUMBER: a burden or hindrance; an encumbering weight; that which impedes or oppresses.
webster_full: CUMBER, v.t. To burden; to obstruct; to oppress with hindrance.
CUMBRANCE, n. A burden; an encumbering weight; a hindrance.
Deuteronomy 1: Moses names the people's strife as an unbearable cumbrance.
Leads directly to the appointment of delegated, plural leadership.
Establishes a pattern echoed in Exodus 18 and Acts 6.
scriptures: Deu 1:12
How can I myself alone bear your cumbrance, and your burden, and your strife?
corruption_summary: A leadership culture that concentrates all authority and burden in a single figure, whether out of ambition or false humility refusing to delegate, repeats exactly the unsustainable cumbrance Moses rightly refused to bear alone.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation it names — a single leader shouldering a burden meant to be shared — recurs in every generation's church and civic life, whether from pride, mistrust of others, or simple failure to plan.

The principle to recover is Moses' own solution: wise, understanding, known men appointed as heads over divisions of the people (Deu 1:13-15). Plurality of leadership, whether elders in a local church or appointed officers in a nation, is Scripture's wise and repeated answer to the cumbrance of concentrated, unshared burden.
roots_summary: Old French combrer, to hinder or obstruct, likely of Gaulish origin, stands behind both cumber and encumber; cumbrance names, at root, an obstructing weight that blocks free movement or action.
roots_lines: Combrer in Old French means to hinder or obstruct.
Cumbrance is an obstructing, encumbering weight.
Deuteronomy applies it to the burden of governing a quarrelsome people.
Leads to the appointment of delegated, plural leadership.
Establishes a biblical pattern echoed throughout Scripture.
usage: How can I myself alone bear your cumbrance, and your burden, and your strife? — the burden of ungoverned strife.
Leads directly to the appointment of plural, delegated leadership.
Echoed in Exodus 18 and the appointment of deacons in Acts 6.

pos: adv. (skillfully; in an archaic sense, with learned craft or artful contrivance)
etymology: From Old English cunnan, to know, be able; cunning originally meant knowledge or skill before narrowing to its modern sense of crafty deceit.
biblical_def:
For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.

Peter defends the apostolic testimony against any charge that it rests on cleverly invented myth, insisting instead on direct eyewitness experience of Christ's majesty, almost certainly referring to the Transfiguration he goes on to describe (2Pe 1:17-18). Cunningly devised fables names precisely the kind of elaborate, artfully constructed mythology that pagan religion and, later, gnostic speculation often produced, and Peter's blunt denial, we have not followed, sets apostolic testimony in a category entirely apart from such invention. This verse is foundational to the dictionary's own historical confidence: the gospel rests not on literary artistry but on the plain, sworn testimony of men who saw, heard, and touched (1Jn 1:1) the incarnate Word, a testimony Peter backs with his own life, since he would shortly die for a story he had every opportunity and motive to recant had it been invented.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CUNNING: skillfully; with learned craft, art, or ingenious contrivance (archaic, without the modern pejorative sense of deceit alone).
webster_full: CUNNING, a. Skillful; knowing; artful; possessing learned craft.
CUNNINGLY, adv. With skillful or artful contrivance.
2 Peter 1: apostolic testimony denied to be cunningly devised fables.
Grounded instead in direct eyewitness testimony of Christ's majesty.
Apostles sealed this testimony with their own lives, even unto death.
scriptures: For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
corruption_summary: Historical-critical scholarship that treats the Gospel accounts as later, artfully constructed myth repeats exactly the charge Peter's own eyewitness testimony was written to refute.
corruption_paragraphs: Form-critical and mythicist approaches to the Gospels often propose that the apostolic testimony to Christ's resurrection and majesty developed gradually as community legend, a cunningly devised fable built up over decades rather than reported directly by eyewitnesses.

2 Peter 1:16 confronts this directly, and in the first person: we have not followed... but were eyewitnesses. The apostolic claim is not literary artistry but sworn, costly testimony, a claim the entire New Testament canon reasserts (Luk 1:1-4; 1Jn 1:1-3) and which the apostles' willingness to die for it rather than recant underwrites.
roots_summary: Old English cunnan, to know or be able, is the root of cunning; the word originally carried the neutral or even honorable sense of skilled knowledge before narrowing, over centuries, toward its modern association with crafty deceit.
roots_lines: Cunnan, to know or be able, is the Old English root.
Cunning originally named skilled knowledge, not deceit alone.
2 Peter denies apostolic testimony is cunningly devised fable.
Grounded instead in direct eyewitness testimony of Christ.
Sealed by the apostles' own costly, sworn commitment to its truth.
usage: We have not followed cunningly devised fables — apostolic testimony, not invented myth.
We were eyewitnesses of his majesty — direct, firsthand testimony.

pos: v. past (thickened or coagulated, as milk forms into curds)
etymology: From Middle English crudden, related to curd, perhaps from Latin crudus, raw, in reference to coagulated milk.
biblical_def:
Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese?

Job's complaint in this chapter traces his own formation in the womb back to God's direct, intimate craftsmanship, using the vivid image of milk poured out and curdled into cheese to describe the gradual, deliberate shaping of flesh, bone, and sinew from formless substance into a structured human body. The image is not flattering in isolation, likening human origin to something as humble as dairy processing, yet Job uses it precisely to press his complaint: the same God who formed him with such intimate, patient care (thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews, Job 10:11) now seems, in Job's affliction, to be hunting him as a fierce lion (Job 10:16). The curdling image therefore serves Job's larger argument throughout the book: a sufferer's bewilderment does not deny God's intimate, sovereign craftsmanship in forming him, but rather intensifies the anguish of apparently losing that same careful God's favor, a tension the whirlwind speeches will later address without ever fully resolving on Job's own terms.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CURDLE: to turn into curd; to coagulate, as milk; to congeal or thicken.
webster_full: CURDLE, v.i./v.t. To turn into curd; to coagulate or congeal.
CURDLED, pp. Thickened into curd; coagulated.
Job 10: God's formation of Job pictured as milk curdled into cheese.
An image of intimate, deliberate, patient divine craftsmanship.
Deepens, rather than denies, Job's anguish over his present affliction.
scriptures: Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese?
corruption_summary: Reading Job's vivid complaints as accusations that God is capricious or cruel, rather than as the honest lament of a sufferer who never once denies God's sovereignty or intimate craftsmanship, misreads the book's own theology.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation in reading Job's speeches is to hear in them a settled theological conclusion about God's character, rather than the honest, anguished protest of a righteous sufferer wrestling in real time.

The principle to recover is the book's own frame (Job 1:22; 42:7-8): Job's raw complaints, including this image of curdled cheese, are never condemned as sin against God's character, and God himself ultimately vindicates Job's honesty over his friends' false comfort, while still correcting Job's presumption in the whirlwind speeches.
roots_summary: Middle English crudden, related to curd, possibly from Latin crudus, raw or uncooked — curdling names the natural thickening of raw milk into a solid mass, a homely image Job presses into theological service.
roots_lines: Crudden in Middle English relates to curd and coagulation.
Curdling names milk's natural thickening into solid mass.
Job applies the image to his own intimate formation by God.
Pictures deliberate, patient divine craftsmanship, not accident.
Deepens rather than denies the anguish of Job's present affliction.
usage: Poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese — intimate divine craftsmanship.
Deepens, rather than resolves, Job's honest anguish in suffering.
God never condemns Job's honest complaint as sin against him.

pos: adv. (skillfully, with intricate and careful craftsmanship; archaically, not merely inquisitively)
etymology: From Latin curiosus, careful, diligent, from cura, care; the older sense emphasizes careful workmanship rather than mere inquisitiveness.
biblical_def:
My substance was not hid from thee, when I was made in secret, and curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth.

David's meditation on God's exhaustive knowledge of him turns, in this verse, to his own formation in the womb, pictured as curiously wrought, skillfully and intricately crafted, in the lowest parts of the earth, a poetic figure for the hidden, secret place of the womb itself. Far from a merely inquisitive glance, curiously here carries its older, stronger sense of careful, expert craftsmanship, the same sense preserved in phrases like a curious work of art; God is pictured as an intricate artisan fashioning every hidden detail of a human being before any other eye can see it. This verse stands among Scripture's clearest affirmations of the unborn child's full personhood and God's intimate, individual craftsmanship from the earliest, most hidden stage of life, undergirding the dictionary's unwavering commitment to the sanctity of life from conception, since the very substance later called me was already known, named, and curiously wrought by God before birth, before sight, before any human witness at all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CURIOUS: skillfully; with careful, intricate workmanship (archaic sense, distinct from modern inquisitiveness).
webster_full: CURIOUS, a. Made with care and art; wrought with nice skill; intricate.
CURIOUSLY, adv. With careful, skillful, intricate craftsmanship.
Psalm 139: the psalmist's own body curiously wrought in the womb.
Pictures God as an intimate, expert artisan of hidden human life.
A foundational text for the sanctity of life from conception.
scriptures: My substance was not hid from thee, when I was made in secret, and curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth.
corruption_summary: Abortion-rights arguments that locate full personhood only at some later developmental stage or at birth directly contradict this psalm's affirmation that God's intimate, careful craftsmanship and full knowledge of a person begin in the secret, hidden place of the womb.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern arguments for abortion frequently propose that personhood, or at least morally significant personhood, develops gradually and is not fully present in early or even later prenatal life, treating the unborn as potential rather than actual persons known and named by God.

Psalm 139:15-16 directly opposes this framework: my substance was not hid from thee when curiously wrought in secret, and in thy book all my members were written, when as yet there was none of them. The unborn child is fully known, fully individual, and fully the object of God's intimate craftsmanship from the earliest hidden stage, grounding the dictionary's unwavering commitment to the sanctity of life from conception.
roots_summary: Latin curiosus, careful or diligent, derives from cura, care — curiously in its older sense names the quality of careful, attentive craftsmanship, a meaning largely displaced in modern English by the narrower sense of mere inquisitiveness.
roots_lines: Cura, care, underlies curiosus and English curious.
Curiously in its older sense names careful, skillful craftsmanship.
Psalm 139 applies it to God's formation of the unborn.
Pictures intimate, expert divine artisanship, not mere chance.
Grounds the full personhood and dignity of the unborn child.
usage: Curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth — careful divine craftsmanship, not accident.
My substance was not hid from thee — full personhood from the hidden, earliest stage.
Foundational for the sanctity of life from conception.

pos: v. past (failed or refused to obey; acted contrary to a given command)
etymology: From dis-, a negating prefix, and obey, from Latin obedire, to give ear to, obey.
biblical_def:
And he cried unto the man of God that came from Judah, saying, Thus saith the LORD, Forasmuch as thou hast disobeyed the mouth of the LORD, and hast not kept the commandment which the LORD thy God commanded thee.

This solemn pronouncement falls on the unnamed man of God from Judah who had faithfully delivered a true prophetic word against Jeroboam's altar at Bethel, under an explicit divine command not to eat bread, drink water, or return by the way he came. An old prophet of Bethel, lying to him that an angel had given a contrary instruction, deceives the man of God into disobedience, and the judgment that follows (he is killed by a lion on the road) falls despite the disobedience being the product of another's deception, not willful rebellion. This troubling episode teaches a hard but necessary lesson the dictionary will not soften: a direct command from the LORD is not nullified by another person's claimed, contrary revelation, however plausible or even prophetic-sounding that other voice may seem, and obedience to God's own clear word takes precedence over any subsequent claim, however sincerely offered, that would lead one away from it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DISOBEY: to neglect or refuse obedience; to violate a command or injunction.
webster_full: DISOBEY, v.t. To neglect or refuse to obey; to transgress a command.
DISOBEYED, pp. Violated by refusal or neglect of obedience.
1 Kings 13: the man of God disobeys the LORD's explicit command.
Deceived into disobedience by a false prophetic claim from another.
Judgment falls despite the disobedience arising from deception, not rebellion.
scriptures: And he cried unto the man of God that came from Judah, saying, Thus saith the LORD, Forasmuch as thou hast disobeyed the mouth of the LORD, and hast not kept the commandment which the LORD thy God commanded thee,
corruption_summary: A relativized view of spiritual authority that treats any sincerely claimed revelation as equally weighty, regardless of its conflict with God's already-revealed, explicit command, repeats the old prophet of Bethel's deceptive error and the younger prophet's fatal credulity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word, but the passage's lesson addresses a perennial danger: treating a later, contrary claim of revelation as automatically trumping an already clear command from God.

The principle to recover is 1 Kings 13's own hard lesson: the man of God should have held fast to the LORD's explicit word to him regardless of the old prophet's contrary claim. Any later voice, however plausible, that contradicts Scripture's settled commands must be tested and rejected (1Jn 4:1), not obeyed merely because it claims angelic or prophetic authority.
roots_summary: Latin obedire, to give ear to or obey, lies behind obey; disobeyed simply negates this with the prefix dis-, naming a refusal to give the ear and the will to a command already heard and understood.
roots_lines: Obedire, to give ear to, is the Latin root of obey.
Dis- negates it, naming a refusal of heard command.
1 Kings 13 applies it to a prophet deceived into disobedience.
Judgment falls despite the disobedience stemming from deception.
Teaches that a later claimed revelation cannot override God's clear word.
usage: Thou hast disobeyed the mouth of the LORD — a command violated despite deception, not willful rebellion.
Deceived by an old prophet's false claim of angelic revelation.
God's explicit prior word takes precedence over any later contrary claim.

pos: n. plural (scatterings; the state or periods of a people being scattered among the nations)
etymology: From Latin dispergere, to scatter abroad, from dis-, apart, and spargere, to scatter, sprinkle.
biblical_def:
Howl, ye shepherds, and cry; and wallow yourselves in the ashes, ye principal of the flock: for the days of your slaughter and of your dispersions are accomplished; and ye shall fall like a pleasant vessel.

Jeremiah's oracle targets the shepherds, the political and religious leaders of Judah and the surrounding nations, pronouncing the appointed days of your slaughter and of your dispersions as accomplished, that is, as having fully come due, their measure of judgment complete. The dispersions in view are the coming exiles, the scattering of leaders and people alike among foreign lands as covenant judgment for persistent unfaithfulness, a theme Jeremiah develops at length throughout his prophecy. The vivid image, ye shall fall like a pleasant vessel, pictures something precious and finely made shattering suddenly and completely, the very leaders who should have guarded the flock becoming instead broken pottery scattered among the nations. Jeremiah's larger prophetic ministry holds this severe judgment together with genuine hope of future restoration (Jer 29:10-14; 31:31-34), a pattern of discipline followed by covenant renewal that the dictionary traces throughout Israel's history as the LORD's consistent dealing with his covenant people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DISPERSE: the act or state of being scattered abroad; a scattering of a people among various places or nations.
webster_full: DISPERSE, v.t. To scatter in different directions; to spread abroad.
DISPERSION, n. The act or state of being scattered; a scattering abroad.
Jeremiah 25: Judah's shepherds face appointed days of dispersions.
Pictures a precious vessel shattering suddenly and completely.
Held together with genuine hope of future covenant restoration.
scriptures: Howl, ye shepherds, and cry; and wallow yourselves in the ashes, ye principal of the flock: for the days of your slaughter and of your dispersions are accomplished; and ye shall fall like a pleasant vessel.
corruption_summary: Reading the exile purely as a geopolitical misfortune, detached from Jeremiah's own insistence that it is covenant discipline for unfaithfulness, strips the dispersions of their actual theological meaning.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation here is historical-critical minimalism, treating the Babylonian exile as mere ancient power politics with no covenantal significance.

The principle to recover is Jeremiah's own repeated framing: the dispersions are the LORD's appointed judgment on unfaithful shepherds and people (Jer 25:4-7), discipline measured out in holiness, not accident, and held together throughout the book with the LORD's unbroken promise of eventual restoration and a new covenant (Jer 31:31-34).
roots_summary: Latin dispergere compounds dis-, apart, with spargere, to scatter or sprinkle — dispersion names a scattering apart, the same root that gives the later technical term diaspora for Israel's scattering among the nations.
roots_lines: Dis-, apart, and spargere, to scatter, form dispergere.
Dispersion names a scattering apart among many places.
Jeremiah applies it to the coming exile of Judah's leaders.
Pictures a precious vessel shattering suddenly and completely.
Held together with the LORD's promise of future restoration.
usage: The days of your slaughter and of your dispersions are accomplished — appointed covenant judgment.
Ye shall fall like a pleasant vessel — sudden, complete shattering.
Held together with Jeremiah's promise of eventual restoration.

pos: v. past (unfurled, spread out, or set up openly for public sight; raised as a visible standard)
etymology: From Old French despleier, to unfold, from Latin displicare, to scatter, unfold, from dis- and plicare, to fold.
biblical_def:
Thou hast given a banner to them that fear thee, that it may be displayed because of the truth. Selah.

This verse sits in a psalm recalling past deliverance and present confidence amid continuing national trouble, and the image is unmistakably military: a banner, a rallying standard around which an army gathers, given by God himself to those that fear him, displayed, raised visibly, because of the truth. The banner is not raised for its own glory but because of the truth, publicly testifying to the reliability of God's covenant word and past faithfulness even in the midst of present affliction (Psa 60:1-3). Displayed carries the sense of deliberate, open, rallying visibility, an emblem meant to be seen by friend and foe alike, gathering God's people around a shared confidence in his truth rather than their own strength. The psalm's closing confidence, through God we shall do valiantly (Psa 60:12), flows directly from this displayed banner: a people who rally not around their own might but around God's proven, truthful word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DISPLAY: unfurled; spread open to view; exhibited publicly, as a banner or standard.
webster_full: DISPLAY, v.t. To unfold; to spread wide; to exhibit openly to view.
DISPLAYED, pp. Unfurled and set up for open, public sight.
Psalm 60: a banner displayed because of the truth, for God's fearers.
A rallying standard testifying to God's reliability, not human strength.
Grounds the psalm's closing confidence in valiant, God-given action.
scriptures: Psa 60:4
Thou hast given a banner to them that fear thee, that it may be displayed because of the truth. Selah.
corruption_summary: Nationalist or triumphalist movements that display banners and symbols chiefly for self-glorification, rather than as public testimony to God's revealed truth, invert the purpose Psalm 60 explicitly assigns to the banner it describes.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation in any age is to raise rallying symbols for the glory of a nation, movement, or self, borrowing the language of banners and standards while detaching them from any grounding in revealed truth.

The principle to recover is the psalm's own phrase: displayed because of the truth. Any banner God's people raise, whether literal or figurative, is rightly raised only in testimony to his proven faithfulness and truth, not as a vehicle for human pride or triumphalism (Psa 115:1).
roots_summary: Latin displicare, to unfold or scatter, compounds dis- with plicare, to fold — to display is, at root, to unfold something that was folded, making it visible and open where it had been hidden or gathered.
roots_lines: Dis-, apart, and plicare, to fold, form displicare.
To display is to unfold what was hidden or gathered.
Psalm 60 applies it to a God-given rallying banner.
Raised publicly because of the truth, not human strength.
Grounds the psalm's confidence in God's proven faithfulness.
usage: A banner... that it may be displayed because of the truth — public testimony to God's faithfulness.
A rallying standard, not a vehicle for human pride.
Grounds the psalm's closing confidence in God-given valor.

pos: n. (a formal dispute or debate; contentious argument over a disputed matter)
etymology: From Latin disputatio, a discussion, debate, from disputare, to examine, discuss, dispute.
biblical_def:
When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.

This disputation, no small dissension, erupted at Antioch when certain men from Judea insisted that Gentile converts must be circumcised according to the Mosaic law to be saved, striking directly at the gospel's core claim of salvation by grace through faith alone. The church's response to this serious doctrinal disputation models the proper biblical pattern for resolving it: not mere local argument left unsettled, but a formal referral to the apostles and elders gathered at Jerusalem, resulting in the Jerusalem Council's definitive ruling preserved in Acts 15. The disputation, however sharp, served the truth rather than fracturing the church, because it was pursued through legitimate, ordered church authority rather than factional division. This episode stands as the New Testament's own template for how doctrinal dispute, even over matters as fundamental as the terms of salvation, is to be pursued: vigorously contended for, yet resolved through the church's appointed, orderly process rather than schism.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DISPUTE: a formal debate or argument; contention, especially over a doctrinal or legal question.
webster_full: DISPUTE, v.i. To argue; to contend in words; to debate a disputed point.
DISPUTATION, n. A formal debate or argument; serious contention.
Acts 15: sharp disputation at Antioch over circumcision and salvation.
Resolved through referral to the apostles and elders at Jerusalem.
Models vigorous doctrinal contention pursued through ordered church authority.
scriptures: Act 15:2

When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.
corruption_summary: A false-peace ecclesiology that treats all doctrinal disputation as itself the problem, prizing surface unity over resolving a serious error, would have left the Judaizing heresy unanswered at Antioch rather than referred to Jerusalem for a definitive ruling.
corruption_paragraphs: Some contemporary church cultures treat any vigorous doctrinal disputation as inherently divisive and therefore to be avoided, prioritizing a surface harmony that tolerates serious error rather than contending for the truth.

Acts 15 commends the opposite pattern: Paul and Barnabas pursued no small dissension and disputation precisely because the gospel's terms were at stake, and the church's maturity is shown not in avoiding the dispute but in resolving it rightly, through ordered apostolic authority, producing a clear, written, binding ruling (Act 15:22-29) rather than lingering ambiguity.
roots_summary: Latin disputare compounds dis-, apart, with putare, to reckon or consider — disputation is, at root, a reckoning things apart, weighing opposing considerations through formal, reasoned argument rather than mere assertion.
roots_lines: Dis-, apart, and putare, to reckon, form disputare.
Disputation is a formal reckoning-apart of opposing views.
Acts 15 applies it to the Antioch dispute over circumcision.
Resolved through referral to apostolic authority at Jerusalem.
Models vigorous contention pursued through ordered church process.
usage: No small dissension and disputation — serious, vigorous doctrinal contention.
Referred to the apostles and elders at Jerusalem for resolution.
Models contending for truth through ordered church authority, not schism.

pos: n. plural (contentious or doubtful arguments, especially over matters of conscience rather than clear doctrine)
etymology: From Latin disputatio, as above, here in its plural form.
biblical_def:
Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.

Paul's instruction in Romans 14 addresses a different category of dispute than Acts 15's circumcision controversy: matters of conscience over food, days, and other disputable practices not clearly settled by apostolic doctrine, which Paul calls doubtful disputations. The weak brother, troubled in conscience over eating meat or observing certain days, is to be received, welcomed into full fellowship, rather than subjected to constant argument meant to force uniformity of practice on matters Scripture itself leaves to individual conscience. This is the crucial distinction the dictionary draws between Acts 15's disputation, rightly pursued because the gospel's terms were at stake, and Romans 14's doubtful disputations, rightly avoided because they concern adiaphora, matters indifferent, where each is to be fully persuaded in his own mind (Rom 14:5). Confusing the two categories, treating disputable matters of Christian liberty as though they were gospel essentials, produces needless division; confusing them the other way, treating gospel essentials as mere disputable preference, produces doctrinal collapse.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DISPUTATION: contentious or doubtful arguments; debates over matters not clearly settled, especially of scruple or conscience.
webster_full: DISPUTATION, n. plural: contentious debates, especially over doubtful or disputable matters.
DOUBTFUL DISPUTATIONS: arguments over matters of conscience, not clear doctrine.
Romans 14: the weak brother received, not subjected to forced uniformity.
Distinguished from Acts 15's disputation over essential gospel terms.
Distinguishes gospel essentials from matters of Christian liberty.
scriptures: Rom 14:1
Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
corruption_summary: Collapsing the biblical distinction between gospel essentials and disputable matters of conscience produces two opposite errors: forcing uniformity on adiaphora, or treating essential doctrine as mere disputable preference.
corruption_paragraphs: Legalistic church cultures often turn Romans 14's disputable matters, diet, days, customs not commanded in Scripture, into tests of fellowship, subjecting weaker consciences to the very doubtful disputations Paul forbids.

An opposite modern error treats genuinely essential doctrines, the deity of Christ, justification by faith, biblical sexuality, as though they too were merely disputable matters of personal conviction. Romans 14 governs adiaphora alone; it supplies no warrant for treating gospel essentials as negotiable, a distinction Galatians 1:8-9 enforces without exception.
roots_summary: Latin disputatio, a discussion or debate, as above; in its Romans 14 usage the word is qualified by doubtful, marking out a specific category of dispute over matters where Scripture itself leaves room for differing conscience.
roots_lines: Disputatio, a formal debate, is the shared Latin root.
Doubtful disputations names arguments over disputable conscience, not doctrine.
Romans 14 commands receiving the weak brother without forced uniformity.
Distinguished sharply from Acts 15's dispute over gospel essentials.
Confusing the two categories produces division or doctrinal collapse.
usage: Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations — welcome without forced uniformity.
Governs adiaphora, matters of conscience, not essential doctrine.
Confusing this with gospel essentials produces division or collapse.
